one_liner: Julia package for incremental 2D Delaunay/Voronoi tessellation; its author's 2014 benchmark had it about 20% faster than CGAL 4.4.
what_it_does: Builds a 2D Delaunay tessellation by pushing points into a DelaunayTessellation, then iterates Delaunay edges, Voronoi edges and triangles, or locates the triangle containing a query point and walks to its neighbours. Points are any AbstractPoint2D subtype from GeometricalPredicates.jl, and every coordinate must lie in [1.0+eps, 2.0-2eps], so callers have to rescale their data first. The API is native Julia (push!, iterators, locate/movea/moveb/movec), with nothing exposed for C or C++.
how_it_is_fast: It does incremental insertion with Lawson edge flips to restore the Delaunay property, following the Arepo paper (arXiv 0901.4107). Bulk push! shuffles the input and then applies a multiscale Hilbert sort (mssort!), so each point lands near the previous one and the walk to its triangle stays short. Predicates come from GeometricalPredicates.jl, which filters in Float64 with bounded error and falls back to exact BigInt arithmetic. The fixed [1,2) coordinate range gives a constant exponent, so each mantissa maps one-to-one onto an integer. Triangles are mutable structs in one preallocated vector (sizehint!), and they cache their predicate terms.
when_to_use: You work in Julia and need a 2D Delaunay or Voronoi tessellation of thousands to millions of points without depending on CGAL.
Points are roughly uniform and can be affinely rescaled into [1,2]^2 without any loss of meaning.
You insert points incrementally and need point location plus neighbour walking on a live tessellation.
You want Voronoi edges for plotting or mesh generation from images (from_image), and approximate results on degenerate inputs are acceptable.
when_not_to_use: Your project is C or C++. This is Julia-only, and the C++ siblings (pgl, Delaunay32, detria) can be linked directly.
You need weighted (power) diagrams, constrained edges, 3D tessellations or Lloyd relaxation. The README lists all of these as unimplemented.

Inputs are small or degenerate. Open issues report no triangles or edges for 3-4 points or collinear points (#55, #51), a triangle union that does not match the convex hull (#34), and an indefinite hang in push! on an 81-point set (#38).
Memory is tight. The author's gist measured about 2-3x CGAL's memory use.
You need an actively maintained library. The README itself recommends DelaunayTriangulation.jl instead.

integration.platforms: any platform Julia runs on (pure Julia, no native code)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; push! mutates the tessellation, so build it from one task

gotchas: Coordinates outside [1.0+eps, 2.0-2eps] are not checked by push!. Out-of-range points break the predicates, and inserting (0.0, 0.0) hung forever in closed issue #36.
push!(tess, array) shuffles and Hilbert-sorts the caller's array in place, so the input order is lost.
Duplicate points are not handled. GeometricalPredicates assumes vertices never overlap, so callers must deduplicate.

Iteration skips every triangle that touches the four auxiliary corner points. This is the likely reason small or collinear inputs yield no triangles or edges (issues #55, #51) and hull triangles can go missing (#34).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only inside a Julia codebase. For C++, pgl (measured against CGAL 6.1.2 Delaunay_triangulation_2), Delaunay32 (multithreaded, beats Triangle and Fade2D) or detria (constrained) are callable directly and have more recent evidence, and jc_voronoi covers plain 2D Voronoi in C.
verified_claims_summary: In 2014 the package author inserted 10K to 10M uniform points (5 runs each) on an Intel Core i7-4800MQ under Windows 8, with Julia 0.3.0 against CGAL 4.4 built with VS2013 64-bit release, and reported about 20% faster construction at 2-3x CGAL's memory. The timings exist only as a graph image. CGAL's time includes memory allocation while Julia's storage was preallocated, so the margin is partly an allocation effect.
status_note: In maintenance mode, with the last commit on 2023-06-28 and the README pointing users to DelaunayTriangulation.jl. It is MIT-licensed, about 760 lines and easy to read, but several correctness issues remain open.
